module_title: Atomic Structure: Early Models and Bohr's Theory (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: This foundational level traces the evolution of our understanding of the atom, from Dalton's indivisible sphere to Rutherford's nuclear model, and finally to Bohr's revolutionary quantum model. It heavily focuses on the mathematical derivations for hydrogen-like species, which are massive score-yielders in NEET and JEE Main.

core_concepts.title: Subatomic Particles and Early Models
core_concepts.description: Atoms consist of Protons ($p^+$), Neutrons ($n^0$), and Electrons ($e^-$). J.J. Thomson discovered the electron (Plum Pudding Model). Rutherford's $\alpha$-particle scattering experiment proved that the atom is mostly empty space, with all its positive charge and almost all its mass concentrated in a tiny central 'Nucleus'. The radius of the atom is $\sim 10^{-10} \text{ m}$ (Angstrom), while the nucleus is $\sim 10^{-15} \text{ m}$ (Fermi).

core_concepts.title: Electromagnetic Radiation and Planck's Quantum Theory
core_concepts.description:
Electromagnetic waves are characterized by wavelength ($\lambda$), frequency ($
u$), and wave number ($ ar{
u} = 1/\lambda$). The speed of light is $c = 
u\lambda$. Max Planck proposed that electromagnetic energy is emitted or absorbed discontinuously in discrete packets called 'Quanta' (or 'Photons' for light). The energy of one quantum is $E = h
u =  rac{hc}{\lambda}$, where $h = 6.626 	imes 10^{-34} 	ext{ J s}$.

core_concepts.title: Bohr's Model for Hydrogen-like Species
core_concepts.description:
Niels Bohr applied quantum theory to Rutherford's model for single-electron systems ($H, He^+, Li^{2+}$). Postulates: 
1. Electrons revolve in stationary circular orbits without radiating energy.
2. Angular momentum is quantized: $mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$.
3. Energy is absorbed or emitted only when an electron jumps between orbits: $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = h\nu$.

core_concepts.title: Mathematical Formulation of Bohr's Orbits
core_concepts.description:
For an electron in the $n$-th orbit of a species with atomic number $Z$:
1. Radius: $r_n = 0.529 \times \frac{n^2}{Z} \text{ \AA}$.
2. Velocity: $v_n = 2.18 \times 10^6 \times \frac{Z}{n} \text{ m/s}$.
3. Total Energy: $E_n = -13.6 \times \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV/atom}$. (Note: $KE = -E_n$ and $PE = 2E_n$).

core_concepts.title: Hydrogen Emission Spectrum
core_concepts.description: When excited electrons fall back to lower energy levels, they emit photons, creating a line spectrum. The wavelength of the emitted line is given by the Rydberg Formula: $\bar{\nu} = \frac{1}{\lambda} = R_H Z^2 \left( \frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2} \right)$, where $R_H = 109677 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Series names based on $n_1$: Lyman ($n_1=1$, UV), Balmer ($n_1=2$, Visible), Paschen ($n_1=3$, IR), Brackett ($n_1=4$, IR), Pfund ($n_1=5$, IR).

important_entities.name: Ionization Energy (IE)
important_entities.significance: The minimum energy required to completely remove an electron from its ground state to infinity. For Hydrogen, $IE = 13.6 \text{ eV}$. Separation Energy is similar but applies to removing an electron from an excited state (e.g., $n=2$ to $\infty$).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In multiple-choice questions, examiners frequently mix up the proportionalities of Bohr parameters. Always double-check: Radius is directly proportional to $n^2/Z$. Energy is proportional to $Z^2/n^2$. Velocity is proportional to $Z/n$. Mixing these up will instantly lead to the wrong ratio.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
For Hydrogen, memorize the exact energy differences for the first few transitions from $n=1$ to save massive calculation time: 
$n=1 \rightarrow 2$: $\Delta E = 10.2 \text{ eV}$ 
$n=1 \rightarrow 3$: $\Delta E = 12.09 \text{ eV}$ 
$n=1 \rightarrow 4$: $\Delta E = 12.75 \text{ eV}$.

exam_strategy_tips: To find the maximum number of spectral lines emitted when a large sample of H-atoms falls from the $n$-th excited state to the ground state, use the combination formula: $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. Note: If the question says '$n$-th excited state', the principal quantum number is actually $(n+1)$.
